text.p: These are the main stories in Latvian newspapers on Wednesday. Prepared for Reuters by the Co-operation Fund. Reuters has not verified these reports and does not vouch for their accuracy:
- The government decided to set up a special centre at Talsi for the survivors of the weekend tragedy, which claimed the lives of eight children.

- Agriculture Minister Robert Dilba resigned after the prosecutor's office concluded that he had breached the anti-corruption law. The Farmers Union party will today discuss new candidates to the post.
- A bomb-scare emptied the Metropole and Latvia hotels for a few hours on Wednesday. A man said he was protesting against their privatisation by Norwegian Varner Baltija.
- The state labour inspection board said the Talsi firefighters crane had passed technical check-ups.

- Politicians of leading parties, Latvia's Way, Democratic Party Saimnieks, For Fatherland and Freedom/LNNK, said they hoped the government would continue its work despite the resignation of four ministers.
- Prime Minister Andris Shkele has not yet decided when Interior Minister Dainis Turlais should step down.

- The left-wing Latvian Social Democratic party said it may bring an action against Lattelekom on behalf of its analogue telephone network clients, who will be asked to pay for local calls from August 1 without being offered new services.

- The newspaper continues its investigation into the privatisation of the Dauteks chemical fibre plant in Daugavpils. Documents obtained by the newspaper allegedly prove that the factory may have been forced into bankruptcy by international corporations.
- Latvia and Norway are to sign the agreement on visa-free travel as the foreign ministers of the Baltic Sea states meet in Riga.
